sourceTitle: Asteroids: A Question of Risk, Not Panic
scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: EN/B2 independently authored Asteroids test: uncertainty, evidence and planetary-defence reasoning. Human content review pending.

tabs.title: Interpreting the evidence
tabs.description: Read between the lines and establish the main argument.

tabs.title: Evidence in practice
tabs.description: Transfer scientific reasoning to new situations.

questions.q: Why does the writer object to headlines that describe an asteroid as 'heading towards Earth'?
choices: They may turn an ordinary approach into an impression of imminent impact.
They usually refer to objects that do not exist.
They place too much emphasis on the size of the asteroid belt.
They fail to explain why asteroids orbit the Sun.
questions.explanation: The opening separates proximity from a calculated collision probability and cautions that 'near' is misleading in everyday terms.

questions.q: What does a revised orbital estimate most strongly indicate in the writer's account?
choices: The object has suddenly changed its direction without a cause.
The first detection was not an asteroid at all.
Additional evidence is narrowing an earlier range of possibilities.
Astronomers have been using different laws of physics.
questions.explanation: Successive observations improve orbit estimates; changing numbers reflect revised evidence rather than random guessing.

questions.q: What makes the rise and subsequent fall of the 2024 YR4 estimate scientifically understandable?
choices: The telescope measurements were deliberately kept secret at first.
Uncertainty can initially admit a concerning possibility before later observations exclude it.
The predicted collision date was constantly moved to a later year.
A threatening object must become harmless after a fixed number of weeks.
questions.explanation: The initially uncertain orbit admitted impact possibilities that were ruled out by later measurements.

questions.q: Which qualification is essential when discussing the DART experiment?
choices: The mission proved it is impossible to influence a space object's motion.
The target was about to collide with Earth before the experiment.
The experiment cannot be measured because it occurred in space.
A successful change in one orbit does not establish a universal defence solution.
questions.explanation: The experiment showed a feasible change, not that every potential impact can be prevented regardless of composition or warning time.

questions.q: Why should an early risk estimate be reported together with its uncertainty?
choices: An isolated number may appear more definite than the available data justify.
It allows journalists to calculate the asteroid's exact composition.
It proves that further measurements are unnecessary.
It makes the probability easier to remember.
questions.explanation: The writer argues that a dramatic probability divorced from its uncertainty misleads readers.

questions.q: What is the rhetorical purpose of the 2024 YR4 case?
choices: To argue that February forecasts should never be trusted.
To demonstrate how headlines can race ahead of changing scientific evidence.
To show that impact predictions are always false.
To prove that all large asteroids are visible well before an approach.
questions.explanation: The example traces a moving estimate and its publicity to illustrate the normal refinement of orbit predictions.

questions.q: Why might years of routine observation be more useful than a spectacular last-minute response?
choices: Spacecraft are less accurate than ordinary telescopes in every case.
Public communication matters only after a predicted collision.
Reliable early information creates time for proportionate decisions and preparation.
Large impacts are certain to happen within a few years.
questions.explanation: The article repeatedly connects effective defence to early discovery, uncertainty reduction and cooperative planning.

questions.q: A news site reports a 2% impact probability but gives no date or measurement history. What would the article suggest asking first?
choices: Whether this is a preliminary estimate and what observations support it.
Whether the space rock has already entered Earth's atmosphere.
Whether the quoted percentage can be rounded to zero.
Whether the asteroid has appeared in a science-fiction film.
questions.explanation: A responsible report clarifies how provisional the estimate is and which measurements underlie it.

questions.q: A proposed defence plan assumes DART's result will be identical for every asteroid. What is its chief weakness?
choices: The DART spacecraft was never tested against a real asteroid.
The method can work only when the target is inside Earth's atmosphere.
All future asteroids have been shown to be far smaller than Dimorphos.
An asteroid's structure and the available warning time can change the outcome.
questions.explanation: The experiment does not establish uniform effects across different physical objects and warning times.

questions.q: Which public message best matches the article's conclusion?
choices: Once a spacecraft succeeds, international cooperation becomes unnecessary.
Scientists should avoid discussing uncertainties until they disappear.
Monitoring and revising predictions openly are reasons for preparedness, not panic.
Every close approach should trigger an emergency response.
questions.explanation: The conclusion rejects both complacency and inevitable catastrophe in favour of evidence and cooperation.
